name: Jim Crow laws
summary: The Jim Crow laws were the state and local statutes of the American South, from the end of Reconstruction in 1877 to the 1950s and 60s, that enforced racial segregation in schools, transport, public accommodations and much else, banned interracial marriage, and sat alongside measures that disfranchised Black voters. Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld them under 'separate but equal', although facilities for Black people were inferior or absent. They stand as a body of enacted law, so what they hold is what the statutes required.

scope: The body of Southern state and local laws that enforced racial segregation between 1877 and the civil-rights era, as Britannica (Urofsky) and History.com define them, with the companion measures they name: bans on interracial marriage, and disfranchisement by reading tests, property qualifications and poll taxes. Answers rest on the laws' own record (BlackPast's list of Tennessee statutes) and on Plessy v. Ferguson, which Britannica ties to them. It excludes the Black Codes, the Klan and lynching as such, and Northern informal segregation, which are other subjects.
